dimension_grades.evidence: The email contains no 'no worries if not,' 'even if this isn't a fit,' or similar hedging phrases anywhere in the draft.
'I'd like to spend 30 minutes walking through the unit economics and our expansion data' states the ask in plain language.
The opening line 'I'm raising a Series A for Conduit, and I want to talk to you about leading it' is direct about what the sender wants.
The line 'I think this is a good conversation for both of us' is supported immediately by a substantive reason rather than used as a hollow rapport-builder.
'We didn't have a sales team for the first eleven months... drove us from first design partner to $2.8M in ARR across 40 accounts in fourteen months' places metrics in a clear time-based sequence.
All traction data ($2.8M ARR, 40 accounts, 14 months, no paid acquisition) appears embedded in flowing prose paragraphs, not as a list.
'three enterprise accounts... are pushing us into compliance and governance territory we hadn't planned to enter until next year' implies accelerating momentum without explicitly claiming it.
'Engineers at one company would set it up, move jobs, and install it at their next company' describes clear customer-pull demand rather than company-pushed growth.
'Your piece in First Round Review last year argued that the best developer tools win by becoming invisible' references a specific published article rather than just a deal or title.
The email directly connects Sarah's 'invisible tools' thesis to Conduit's workflow-integration approach and carry-along adoption behavior.
The personalization passage immediately introduces the carry-along behavior metric leading to '$2.8M in ARR across 40 accounts in fourteen months.'
The reference to Sarah's article flows directly into the business description and traction story without standing as a separate flattery paragraph.
The email contains no phrases like 'happy to work around your schedule' or 'whenever works for you'; the closing simply states 'I'm open Tuesday or Thursday afternoon next week.'

'You've been building a thesis around infrastructure that compounds through practitioner loyalty... and we're one of the clearest examples of that thesis playing out' frames the conversation as valuable to both parties.
'I'm open Tuesday or Thursday afternoon next week. What works?' proposes a concrete time window rather than leaving scheduling entirely open-ended.
'$2.8M ARR infrastructure startup' provides a concrete traction and domain credibility signal in the subject line.
'Series A conversation' makes the nature and purpose of the email immediately discernible from the subject line.
The subject line uses standard capitalization, no ellipses, no 're:' faking, and no vague teasers — it is straightforwardly descriptive.
